unresolvedQuestions: ANSWERED, AND IT IS THIS TEAM'S OWN REGRESSION — was the round-16 rim cut the cause of the `wide` blocker? NO for the rim, YES for the round-16 sky change by a different path. (a) THE RIM IS EXONERATED, by ablation on the illuminant arithmetic with everything else held: cutting the rim from the round-15 placement (0.270 of it on horizontal ground in the `wide` pose) to RIM_ELEVATION_DEG = 9 (0.1564) moves the lit plateau illuminant from R/B 1.1577 to 1.1749, i.e. 1.5% WARMER, and the shadow illuminant from 0.3850 to 0.3807, 1.1% cooler. The symptom is a blue shift; the rim cut pushed the lit ground the other way and by a factor of thirty too little. (b) The round-16 chroma restoration reaching the fill is also too small: through the probe's hue it moves the lit illuminant R/B 1.1976 -> 1.1749 (-1.9%) and the shadow 0.3900 -> 0.3807 (-2.4%). Neither term, nor both together, is within an order of magnitude of the frame's measured move. (c) THE PATH IT ACTUALLY TOOK IS THE FOG COLOUR. fogParams.topColor is derived from the dome by _airColor -> _evalSky(raw = false), which includes SKY_CHROMA. Measured on the twin, pre-r16 -> post-r16: (0.2536, 0.3436, 0.4143) R/B 0.6122 -> (0.2075, 0.3466, 0.5504) R/B 0.3771, a 38% collapse in R/B at held luminance (0.3296 -> 0.3317, +0.6%). Every near-field ground-directed ray took 100% of that colour, because nearAir was 1.0 below f = 0.10. So a round-16 change that was correct and desirable on the dome was silently piped into the ground through the aerial-perspective sampler. That is the regression, it is ours, and it is what this round fixes.

WHY IT MATTERS SO MUCH AT ONLY 10% OF THE PIXEL — the airlight colour is sky radiance and the sky is several times brighter than shadowed ground in the same frame, so a 8-12% blend is a large fraction of the pixel's own radiance. The frame-side evidence is a ladder rather than a model: on shots/phone-wide-r16v1.png, eight 60x40 ground-only boxes down one column verified by cropping the whole strip first (crop 0.79,0.63,0.075,0.37 — clean ground end to end), at x-frac 0.815 and y-frac 0.955 / 0.905 / 0.855 / 0.805 / 0.755 / 0.705 / 0.665 / 0.640, unprojecting to 23.4 / 25.4 / 27.9 / 31.2 / 35.4 / 41.1 / 47.4 / 52.4 m and to a computed f of 5.1 / 5.7 / 6.5 / 7.4 / 8.6 / 10.2 / 11.9 / 13.3 %, read R-B = +1.3 / +9.5 / -2.7 / -4.4 / -0.9 / -12.2 / -15.8 / -19.0 and lumaSpread 50.1 / 56.9 / 48.4 / 45.6 / 51.4 / 44.8 / 39.4 / 35.1. Least-squares slope -2.944 code values of R-B per 1% of f, r = -0.92 on n = 8; the spread falls monotonically over the same span. Extrapolated to f = 0 the ground reads R-B about +13, i.e. warm and key-lit. The plateau is not missing its key; the airlight is painting over it.

DISPROVED THIS ROUND, so nobody re-tests them: (i) the directional light-index misalignment — the rim is a non-shadow-casting DirectionalLight and three sorts shadow-casting lights first (node_modules/three/build/three.module.js:7957, lights.sort(shadowCastingAndTexturingLightsFirst)), so the rim can never occupy a cascade slot in the unrolled loop, in any build order. (ii) the seven acceptance boxes are NOT beyond the shadow fade — they sit at a constant view depth of 33.3 m against a MEDIUM fade band of (56.0, 67.9) m, so kagFade is exactly 1 there and the shadow term is fully active. Whatever is wrong on that row, it is not the fade. (iii) fog *quantity* alone does not explain the blue: at 8-12% it is only the colour of the airlight that produces a 46% collapse in code R/B, which is why the fix is a hue change and not a density cut.

ROUTING, WITH ARITHMETIC — criterion (3) of the `wide` blocker ('at least one object shadow must be visible... some box within 40 px of the lantern base, downsun, must read below 36.1') is not reachable from these two files under the standing instruction. The row is at view depth 33.3 m, i.e. cascade 1 of 2. Its bounding sphere solves to r = 87.0 m (the ideal centre 99.07 exceeds the sub-frustum far plane 73.35 and is clamped to it, so the radius becomes the far cap's 73.35 * sqrt(a2) = 85.3, times the 1.02 margin), giving a 174 m ortho box on a 1536 map: 11.3 cm per texel and light.shadow.normalBias = 1.6 texels = 18.1 cm. At a 13-degree sun a normal offset h detaches the shadow along the ground by h / tan(13 deg) = 4.33 h = 78 cm, and a stone-lantern shaft is about 35 cm across — its contact shadow is displaced by more than two of its own widths before the map is sampled, and is about 3 texels wide when it lands. That is cascade coverage/resolution/bias, which rounds 7, 8 and 15 closed off and the round-17 coordinator note reaffirms. If the coordinator wants criterion (3), it needs an explicit exemption to refit cascade 1 for wide framings, dispatched with that exemption stated. Do not route it here again without one.

CORRECTION TO THE PROJECT RECORD — round 16 recorded that the `wide` structure target is unreachable because Lighting already delivers the ratio. That conclusion used a log-log display slope of 0.42, which is wrong at these levels: ACES's toe has a v-squared numerator and is expansive there, not compressive. Pushed through three's actual ACESFilmicToneMapping plus the sRGB OETF (and the answer is exposure-independent, identical at 1.0 and 1.5), a shadow floor at p50 38.7 lit at the rig's own ceiling of 1 + key/fill = 1.845x comes out at p50 65.4 — a span of 26.7 code values against the criterion's 25. So criterion (2) IS satisfiable in principle from the current key/fill; what blocks it is (a) the airlight adding a large common term to lit and shadow alike, and (b) there being no cast shadow at that range at all, which is criterion (3) and is cascade-side. Round 18 should not spend itself raising the key on the strength of round 16's arithmetic.

FINDING 10, ROOT CAUSE, measured rather than guessed: uCloudCoverage is a threshold on a field whose GLOBAL median is 0.500 (mass 0.70 + mid 0.30 of two normalised fbm2 bands, each *0.5+0.5), so 0.455 is correctly authored for roughly half the sky. But at uCloudScale 0.00055 the mass band is sampled at p*0.24 over a span of well under one noise cell per frame, so a whole 62-degree framing sits inside a single trough: over the `torii` visible sky the field reads p1 0.159 / p50 0.320 / p99 0.563 against a threshold at 0.465 that saturates at 0.835. Only the top few per cent of the frame clears it, and the field's own maximum (0.599) reaches only 0.283 of full mass — arithmetically, no cloud anywhere in this frame can exceed 18% opacity. Round 7's fix for confetti overshot from 'one bank spans a large fraction of the sky' to 'one bank does not fit in the sky'.

risks: The near-ground airlight change is deliberately azimuth-independent (uFogColor, not horizonCol). Through horizonCol the fix would have been larger on `wide` but would have taken 65% of the sunward haze (R/B 2.33) onto the near ground of the two frames that look into the sun: priced on `valley`'s fence-shadow box that lands it at R-B +3.6, i.e. a warm shadow, which ARCHITECTURE §5 forbids. Through uFogColor it lands near -6.5. If a later round wants the azimuthal variation in the near field it has to price the sunward frames first.

uCloudScale reaches the PMREM environment bake, because the cube camera renders this same dome material with the deck on. sky.probeIrradiance — what Lighting actually solves against — is sky-only by construction and is unchanged, so the ambient budget cannot move; but the cube's own content gains cloud, which changes the specular environment and the probe's directional shape by an amount that is not measurable without a renderer. Watch for wet stone and the blade reading differently.

The cloud scale is changed globally, not per keyframe. The field's median is a property of fbm2 and not of the hour, so the same 'less than one cell per frame' defect exists at every time of day; a single scale therefore fixes the whole ladder rather than one keyframe. But only t = 0.78 is in the review set, so the other hours are unverified.

Every absolute-level statement in this file that depends on the display transform is model-dependent: three's ACES plus the sRGB OETF, calibrated against two cropped sky directions in `wide`, with PostFX's own grade absent from the model. The ladder slope, the guard-box f values, the illuminant ablation and the deck alpha do NOT depend on it. The '65-99% of the pixel is airlight' figure does, and an inversion at that exposure returns slightly negative surface radiance on the leftmost box, so that figure is over-estimated by perhaps 1.3-1.5x and is quoted only to establish that the airlight is the dominant term, not to give its exact share.

The 7-of-7 prediction is a linear extrapolation of a slope fitted on n = 8 with r = -0.92, over a range of f (5-13%) that brackets the seven boxes (8-12%), so it is an interpolation rather than an extrapolation — but it assumes the ground's own radiance is unchanged, and world/foliage are editing the same plateau this round.
